title: SMSF ban 'would cost 11,500 new homes a year'
full_text:
The government is being urged to wind back its ban on self-managed superannuation funds investing in property, with the housing sector and Coalition warning that the policy would wipe out 11,500 new home builds a year.
With the remaining budget bills scheduled to pass the House of Representatives on Thursday before heading to the Senate in three weeks, the opposition will move an amendment to preserve limited recourse borrowing arrangements for SMSFs purchasing newly built properties.
This would be in line with changes to negative gearing, which, from July 1 next year, will only be allowed for newly built properties purchased after budget night on May 12 this year.
The SMSF push is one of several last-ditch appeals for the government to fix the unintended consequences of its May budget tax hikes, which slapped a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts and scrapped the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount for an inflation-based model with a minimum 30 per cent rate.
Superannuation funds, including SMSFs, were exempt from the budget changes. Super funds are eligible for a 10 per cent tax rate on capital gains when assets are sold and zero tax for retirees aged over 60 when a superannuation fund is in pension phase.
But in June, when the government rushed the first tranche of budget legislation through parliament after a two-day inquiry, the Greens made their support conditional on barring SMSFs from using LRBAs for residential property, arguing this would become a back door to circumvent the budget tax changes.
In Senate estimates on Wednesday, Treasury deputy secretary Katrina Di Marco said that, in 2023-24, about 8700 SMSFs entered into a new limited recourse borrowing arrangement.
This is more than twice the government's claim of 4000 dwellings but still well short of the industry figure of 16,000 investment properties purchased by SMSFs last year.
Work commissioned by the SMSF industry calculated about 11,500 of these were new builds.
Di Marco played down the impact of 8700 fewer dwellings.
"When you look at that in terms of the scale of the overall kind of lending in the economy or activity in the economy, that's less than half a percentage point of new residential borrowing every year," she said. "These are quite small changes."
But Liberal senator and opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg pushed back with a challenge to Finance Minister Katy Gallagher.
"Why would you want to restrain any housing supply in a housing crisis? We just heard from the [Treasury] we might get 180,000 houses [built] in this country this year. We used to get more than 200,000," he said of the annual forecast for housing construction.
"Minister, you did this deal, I think, with the Greens in the Senate. There was no reason undertaken."
Bragg said afterwards the Coalition would seek to amend the bill defining new builds to allow SMSFs to invest in new homes.
"We need every single new home. Sadly, Labor hates investors more than it wants to solve the housing crisis. We just want more homes," he said.
During the estimates hearing, Treasury secretary Jenny Wilkinson stood by her assessment that changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax would have a modest impact on house prices. Wilkinson said dwelling prices had fallen 5.2 per cent from the March peak but remain "almost 6 per cent higher than their levels of a couple of years ago".
Wilkinson said cyclical factors such as high interest rates, heightened global uncertainty, and weak consumer sentiment had contributed to a significant decline in established house prices - while the budget impact was structural.
"The impacts of the tax measures on house prices and rents are expected to be modest over the medium term, while shifting the ownership of the housing stock towards owner-occupiers," she said.
"The most significant impact is coming from four increases in interest rates this year."
Nine Entertainment Co.
author: Phillip Coorey
